Validating a Body-Composition Phenotype-Classification Framework

A worked example: regression and diagnostics, measurement agreement, and out-of-sample classification validity

This short report demonstrates the distinction between training a classifier and validating a classification framework. Using an illustrative cohort of 420 adults with paired measurements of body fat by a reference method and a field proxy metric, it asks a measurement-science question: does the proxy discriminate a high-adiposity phenotype, is it calibrated out-of-sample, and can it substitute for the reference at the individual level?

Methods

Data and phenotype. Paired reference (DXA percent body fat) and proxy measurements were available for 420 adults. The target phenotype, high adiposity, was defined a priori as a reference value of at least 30% body fat (cohort prevalence 50.7%).

Agreement and regression. The proxy was regressed on the reference by ordinary least squares. Regression assumptions were checked with residual-versus-fitted plots and a LOWESS smoother (linearity), the Breusch-Pagan test (homoscedasticity), the Shapiro-Wilk test and a normal Q-Q plot (residual normality), the Durbin-Watson statistic (independence), Cook's distance against a 4/n threshold (influence), and variance inflation factors in the covariate-adjusted model (multicollinearity). Method agreement was quantified with a Bland-Altman analysis (mean bias and 95% limits of agreement), and proportional bias was tested by regressing the paired differences on the paired means.

Classification-framework validation. A logistic model of the phenotype on the proxy was developed on a stratified 60% development sample (n = 252) and applied, unchanged, to the held-out 40% validation sample (n = 168). On the validation sample we estimated discrimination (area under the ROC curve with a 2000-sample bootstrap 95% confidence interval), calibration (calibration curve by decile, calibration slope, calibration-in-the-large, and the Hosmer-Lemeshow test), and an operating point selected by Youden's J. Analyses used Python (numpy, pandas, statsmodels, scipy, matplotlib) under a fixed random seed; the full script is included for reproducibility.

Results

Agreement and diagnostics. The proxy tracked the reference closely (slope 0.97, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.02; R² = 0.775; Pearson r = 0.88). Residuals were approximately normal (Shapiro-Wilk p = 0.626) and showed no serial dependence (Durbin-Watson 1.81), with mild heteroscedasticity (Breusch-Pagan p = 0.041). Cook's distance flagged 17 of 420 observations above the 4/n threshold, and multicollinearity was negligible (maximum VIF 2.41).

Measurement agreement. The mean bias was -0.44 percentage points, but the 95% limits of agreement were wide (-7.0 to 6.1), and a significant proportional bias was present (difference-on-mean slope 0.102, p < 0.001): the proxy increasingly over-reads at higher adiposity.

Out-of-sample classification validity. On the held-out validation sample the framework discriminated the phenotype well (AUC 0.934, 95% CI 0.897 to 0.965) and was adequately calibrated (calibration slope 1.23, calibration-in-the-large -0.07, Hosmer-Lemeshow p = 0.416). At the Youden-optimal threshold (0.44) sensitivity was 0.929 and specificity 0.783.

Interpretation

The proxy discriminates the high-adiposity phenotype strongly and is well calibrated out of sample, so as a classification framework for ranking or triage it is valid. Yet the wide limits of agreement and the proportional bias show it is not interchangeable with the reference for individual-level measurement. That is the core measurement-science point: a framework can be valid for classification while remaining an imperfect measurement instrument, and discrimination alone would hide the gap. A full engagement would add external validation on an independent cohort, decision-curve (net-benefit) analysis, and subgroup checks for construct validity across sex and age.
